title: JSON.parse silently changes a 17-digit integer ID to a different number
assumption: Parsing a JSON number that looks like an integer gives back that exact integer, as long as the JSON text itself is well-formed.

input.description: A large numeric ID - a Snowflake-style ID, a 64-bit database primary key, a big serial number - serialized as a JSON number (not a string) by a backend and consumed by a JavaScript client.

what_goes_wrong: `JSON.parse('{"id": 9007199254740993}').id` returns `9007199254740992` - one less than the actual ID - and re-serializing it with `JSON.stringify` writes back the wrong, rounded value. Python's `json.loads` on the identical text keeps the exact integer.
why: JavaScript's JSON implementation stores every number as the same IEEE-754 double that all JS Numbers use, and doubles can only represent integers exactly up to 2**53 (9,007,199,254,740,992); 9007199254740993 is one past that boundary and rounds to the nearest representable double, which happens to be the even number below it. Python's `json` module parses an integer-looking JSON number into a native arbitrary-precision `int`, which has no such ceiling, so it round-trips exactly.

repros.code:
import json
o = json.loads('{"id": 9007199254740993}')
print(o["id"])
print(o["id"] == 9007199254740993)

fix: Serialize any integer that might exceed 2**53 as a JSON string, not a JSON number, and parse it on the JS side with `BigInt(str)` rather than `JSON.parse`'s default Number conversion. Many JSON APIs for 64-bit IDs (e.g. Twitter/X's `id_str`) already do this for exactly this reason.

sources.title: Python docs: json - JSON encoder and decoder

test_cases.note: their_parse(json_text) must preserve this exact integer id - if it goes through JS's Number type anywhere in the pipeline, it will silently become 9007199254740992.
